en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wushan Duan of Huzhou, composed by Liu Yi, Grand Master of the Left, Minister of War, and Recipient of the Purple Golden Fish Bag.
The Chan Master’s name was Jingduan; his courtesy name was Mingbiao. His clan was Qiu, and his native place was Guian County in Huzhou.
He received his training at Jiekong Monastery on Mount Wu and attained the Dharma from Chan Master Qiye of Longhua Monastery in Lin’an.

Having once visited a patriarch of the school, he suddenly awakened to the full functioning of the mind-ground; his understanding did not dwell in the abstruse, and his insight was sharp and liberated. Although there were three thousand seats in the monastic assemblies, few could match his realization.
He subsequently withdrew to live in seclusion at his home mountain, styling himself Master Anxian. When Yi-xing was about to depart for an official post in the south, [he took leave].
He entered the mountains to pay his respects to his teacher, who presented him with a verse that said: "The Lord of Heaven does not see my faults, Simply because my belly is so vast.
I offer this advice to you, Elder Liu Yi: When serving as an official, act according to this. This was spoken and chanted in mystical and wondrous tones upon a stone cliff within the village.
The poetic verses are numerous; they are all of the same caliber as those of Hanshan and Shide. Containing the ultimate truth in its most authentic form, some are indeed worthy of contemplation.
Because the Master, with his unimpeded eloquence, extensively propagated the Dharma-gift for those with whom he shared a karmic affinity, I have composed this preface.
The Ancient Buddha appeared in the world, practicing both in accordance with and against the flow, amidst winds and waves;
he ascended the mountain four times to universally transform those like Hanshan and Shide, desiring only that people constantly examine themselves and not be drifted away by the eight winds.
When a single thought suddenly accords with reality, that is the moment of arriving home. The Chan Master’s name was Jingduan, his courtesy name Mingbiao, from Guian.
The son of the Qiu family studied at the Jiekong Lecture Hall on Mount Wu. Upon first seeing people performing with a lion, he attained an awakening to the essential point of the mind.
He subsequently visited Chan Master Yue of Cuifeng and attained the Samādhi of Playful Mastery (*yóuxí sānmèi*). He then fashioned a lion skin out of colored silk and wore it as his garment;
thus, this became his title. Throughout his four successive stays in minor monasteries, all were desolate and lacking in provisions, such that people could not endure them.

While others were filled with anxiety, the Master alone found joy; he frequently engaged in playful diversion with worthy scholars and officials, composing verses and hymns that appeared to be mere jests.

Yet upon careful and prolonged contemplation, they were found to contain profound significance. More than a hundred years after his passing into *parinirvāṇa*, these subtle words and deep meanings remain.

This work has long been a favorite among the people. My dharma-grandson, the bhikṣu Shijiao, collected the poems exchanged with scholars and gentlemen during the Master’s lifetime, along with his miscellaneous writings, into a single volume.
He carved woodblocks for its circulation to benefit future generations; his aspiration is truly praiseworthy.
He sought me out to correct errors and omissions, and I could not decline on account of the principle involved. May those who read it look beyond the mere words and characters to perceive the Master.
The Master Fenxun was the venerable master Shijiao; thus, the compilation of this record was not in vain.

Written on the fifth day after the end of autumn in the Jiading Jisi year (1209) by the bhikṣu Dinglong, formerly the abbot of Mount Meichang and a successor in the ancestral lineage, at the East Hall of Tieguanyin.
While I was a guest at Mount Qingliang in Dai, one night I dreamed of a monk wearing a lion’s skin who walked from east to west.
The setting sun hung in the sky, its light illuminating his face. Suddenly he opened his mouth; it was like a basin of blood, and his fangs were like frost-sheathed swords.
In a dream, I privately reflected: "I shall become like him. Upon reading the *Recorded Sayings* of Master Duan, I was struck by how he had cast off all conventional molds;
his great function (*dà yòng*) was纵横 (zōnghéng)—unrestricted and pervasive—leaving no fixed rules behind. Truly, he was like a golden-maned lion leaping and bounding in the open field;
when the various beasts hear its roar, there are none whose brains do not shatter. Alas! Since antiquity has long passed, the [Dharma] lineage...
The gatekeepers and their minions are rarely encountered; they are for the most part like demonic foxes and monstrous dogs.

Soft, supple, and sycophantic, they wag their tails and beg for pity whenever they see anything desirable, employing ten thousand gestures to flatter and accommodate. Once their desires are satisfied, the old man Yama stands before them, shouting and scolding.
If they do not even have the leisure to look back [upon their own origins], how much less will they look back upon my Way?

As for the practice of commenting on ancient cases (*gū*) based on karmic conditions, the compilation of commentaries (*pingchang*) based on those ancient case verses, and the subsequent practice of the so-called "Secret Essentials" (*biyao*) based on those commentaries—if later students do not understand these commentaries, how can they know the ancient case verses?
If they do not know the ancient case verses, how can they know the karmic conditions? If they do not know the karmic conditions...
Because one does not know this, how can one know one’s own mind? If one’s own mind is not known, how can one know the intent of the Patriarchs?

Now, these karmic conditions are but "living words," wherein life and death are exercised with sovereign ease, and suppression or exaltation cannot be fathomed. Here, the paths of ordinary and sage are brought to an end, and right and wrong serve as medicine and disease.
If one is not such a person, the Way will not manifest in vain. Only those who have fully awakened to their own minds can take disease as medicine and medicine as disease.
To kill as soon as life begins; to seize and plunder as soon as one lets go; to suppress only to exalt, and to destroy only to give life.

To take the staff and shouts as a broad and long tongue, and to offer iron nails for rice and wooden shavings for soup as an act of worship. Roaring at the moment of the pivot, the devas and nāgas rejoice while the foxes and hares have their souls withered away.
If this is so, then those who today claim the secret essentials as the authentic transmission are merely arrogant and insulting toward the Dharma.
"Dao! Are you not truly ashamed before your teacher?

Written on the thirteenth day of the second month in the Renchen year of the Wanli era by the monk Zhik'e, known as Daguan Daoren, at Ziken Liao in Miaode An, on the southern slope of Yedou, Mount Wutai.
Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wushan Duan of Huzhou,
Volume One Re-edited by the Dharma-grandson Bhikṣu Sijiao Recorded Sayings of Changxing Shousheng Chan Monastery (Appended: Memorial Requesting the Master to Serve as Abbot by Liu Yiweng)
In the past, Shousheng was not a Chan monastery; monks were rarely seen there. The Rushan mountains have long hidden masters of the Way, who are like ancient Buddhas.

[I] have urgently petitioned the Governor, wishing to obtain a man of high attainment. I respectfully consider that the Master has long awakened to the Mahāyāna and does not cling to minor formalities.
Your wondrous functions are unrestrained, and your coming and going are unhindered. Having thoroughly investigated and turned back, you have overturned the reliance on external support.
Whether speaking coarsely or delicately, all are of the highest capacity; whether eating coarse food or wearing poor clothing, they cultivate only secret practices.

They are accustomed to wandering through cities and towns, yet always laugh and smile amidst forests and springs. With a refined purity that is carefree and elegant gestures that are leisurely, there are white clouds in their empty rooms and the seven fascicles of the Lotus Sutra;
there is the bright moon over the empty pool and the single cry of a fisherman. Given these preferences, how could it be otherwise?
This is not right. If one has become a person, what prevents one from practicing transformation? The hearts of the multitude all rejoice;

they long to pay homage to the Elephant King, whose ten eyes gaze upon him with full vision. They wish to take refuge in the Lion; once their earnest request has been extended, how could humble words suffice?

The Master accepted the invitation. Holding up the letter, he said: "I humbly acknowledge that the official document has arrived, requesting this mountain monk to serve as the abbot of the Shousheng Chan Monastery under the auspices of Mr.
Taiboshi Chengyeweng. Having no way to decline, I shall comply. However, regarding the duties of an abbot, one must strive to move forward.
If I were to come forth to succeed to the ancestral style, it would be difficult to bear the responsibility. Furthermore, my life has been spent in simplicity."
I once traveled on foot, visiting teachers everywhere. At first, I intended to expound upon the sutras and śāstras, but for many years they have fallen into neglect.

As for speaking of the Way or discussing Chan, it is difficult even to open my mouth. Nevertheless, although this is so, matters are not fixed; public authority brooks no partiality, yet private paths allow for the passage of carriages and horses.

He ascended the hall. The Master said: "Maitreya is truly Maitreya; he manifests himself in thousands of billions of bodies. From time to time he shows himself to people of this age, yet these people themselves do not recognize him.
He paused for a long moment and asked: "Is there anyone among you who recognizes him? Come forward and deliver a message. After a long silence, he said:
"Why, O Great Assembly, do you not recognize him? It is simply because he is too near. Sentient beings have long wandered through birth and death; it is precisely because..."
Used daily yet unaware; one has not yet ascended to true awakening and remains constantly in the realm of dreams. An ancient said: "Last night I had a dream; in the dream I saw a mass of emptiness.
This morning, intending to speak of the dream, I looked up and again saw emptiness. Is it that emptiness is the dream, or is it that the dream is emptiness?
I suspect that within this floating life, we are just like being in this very dream. This is what the ancients said.
One Dream. Last night, this mountain monk had a dream that was unlike those of the ancients. In the dream, the local deity said to me:
"Tomorrow, the Great Doctor Cheng and Master Xiongweng will enter the mountains with several others to invite the Abbot to preside over the Shousheng Chan Monastery.
Furthermore, since you, Abbot, have never traveled as a pilgrim, how can you possibly preside over it? The mountain monk replied:
The Path of the Local Deity. Listening to the teachings does not depend on much learning; practicing Chan is not about traveling far and wide.
If one is a true cub of the lion, one can let out a great roar immediately upon birth. The Local Deity asked, "What is a cub of the lion? Is it not so?
Yongjia said: "The lion cub follows the herd; at three years old, it can already let out a great roar.
If a jackal pursues the Dharma King, this hundred-year-old monster merely opens its mouth in vain. How truly marvelous, how truly marvelous! I laugh at myself, this lion cub of the Wu Mountains.
For many years I lay hidden deep within the forest; today I walk slowly forth from the mountain gate, baring my claws and fangs."
Displaying his majestic aura, his two eyes flash with brilliant radiance. Even the blue-eyed barbarian monk does not recognize him;
how then could the local guardian deity or the mountain monk know? While dreaming, he was struck once by the mountain monk’s staff, and the guardian deity suddenly vanished.
O assembly, do not trouble yourselves standing for long. I pray you all take care.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is it like when the wild goat has not yet hung its horns? The Master said, "I am afraid.

The monk pressed further, "What is it like after the wild goat has already hung its horns? Again the Master said, "I am afraid. The monk pressed further, "Since you are a great teacher of goodness (*kalyāṇamitra*), why are you afraid?
The Master said, "I have never seen such a strange beast. The monk withdrew. The Master said, "Today..."
The second day of the second month—what does the Zen elder have to say? The spring breeze touches every eye as a hundred flowers bloom;

the young lords and princes are drunk and tipsy day after day. Only the cypress trees of the Chen dynasty before the palace do not conform to the tastes of the people of this age. O followers of the Zen school!
Simply this—do not give it a thought. After the midday meal, a cup of tea in tranquility; stretching one's legs to sleep upon the long bed.

When Master Biancai arrived, he ascended the hall and raised the verse by Layman Pang: "The ten directions gather together as one; each and every one studies non-action. This is the field for selecting Buddhas;
with an empty mind, they return having passed the imperial examination. This is simply [the teaching] under the gate of Shousheng. Still...
"Is there a passing of the examination, or not? If this mountain monk were to let slip a single thread of leniency, every one of you would possess a lofty name upon the golden list.

But if I were to firmly grasp the heavens and the earth, even if Śākyamuni Buddha and the patriarchs of successive generations were to emerge, each of them would still be nothing more than a scholar who failed the examinations for many years.
After a long silence, he said: "Even the Dharma Master does not appear. He then composed another verse: [Verse omitted per instructions]
The ancients wove their sutras with a single strand of silk, producing exquisite canopies rarely seen in the world. Do not blame this old woman for lacking skill;
it is simply because she did not encounter the right opportunity upon the Dharma Hall.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Long rains have ceased and the weather is fine; the spring breeze harmonizes with all phenomena.

White clouds are originally mindless things, yet they fly from the Southern Mountain over the Northern Slope. Quickly fix your eyes—there is no room for error! In the Hall of Playing with Clouds, we laugh heartily."
Gazing afar at Lake Tai, the waves are still; the fishermen all sing songs of the Great Peace.
On ascending the hall for the New Year, he said: "A new year, a new spring, and the snow grows thick once more; The myriad phenomena of the universe are all the same.
When meeting one another, do not recognize this as such a thing; A full somersault is cast to manifest the ancestral wind. He then performed a somersault and descended from his seat.

From the *Recorded Sayings* of the Great Enlightenment Chan Temple (Dajue Chansi) in Western Yu, the opening address for the formal assembly (*shangtang*) states: "Old Chan Master Duan! Old Chan Master Duan! As abbot, I am carefree and without affliction.

In the morning, I attend the assembly of several dozen monks; At night, I gaze upon the single bright orb of the moon. I exhort all of you to diligently study the Way, And recognize that which is within your robes."
Priceless Treasure. Upon the terrace of Shanguang Hall, the snow has just cleared; the mountain peaks washed clean appear even more magnificent.
Do you all understand? A monk asked, "What is the realm of Xiyu? The Master said, "Scattered and dispersed. The monk pressed further, "What is the person within the realm?
The Master said, "There is no second moon in heaven; in Xiyu there is but one monk. The monk pressed further, "As for the person and the realm..."
Having received the Master’s instruction, [the student] asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master threw down his staff and composed another verse:

"The mountain monk has been dull-witted and clumsy all my life; There is no entanglement to be spoken of. If you ask about the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West, I unfold my bowl twice each day."
Ascending the hall to pray for rain, he said: "The mountain streams flow as if carved open; In a year of drought, we pray for rain to end the people's calamity.
I know not from where the clouds arise, But I see the rain coming down from above. (Immediately it rained.)
The Elder Guangjiao of Xuancheng arrived. He ascended the hall and said: "The floating clouds have dispersed, and the sky is a deep azure;
The spring colors have melted away, and the mountains are even clearer. I cherish this Chan elder, serene as water; He comes at times to accompany me through these remaining years."
The Master arrived at Zhiyuan Temple in Huating. The assembly requested him to ascend the seat, and he said: "Originally a lion of Xiachuan, I have come here to Huating to roar.
There is nothing in the Buddha-dharma to deliberate upon; it is better to perform a somersault. He then performed a somersault.
The assembly took their seats.
Master Lingshan Xiaogao of Xianggao Chan Monastery’s discourse record:
Master Tong Shen-gong and various officials escorted the Master into the monastery. After the incense was offered, the Master rubbed his hands for a long while and sang:
The Fisherman utters a single cry: "Does the Noble Lord hear me? This is the 'Song of Great Peace. He then ascends the seat, picks up his whisk, and looks out over the fourfold assembly, saying:
"By imperial decree of the Three Courts, I am stationed at Lingfeng; amidst the dense array of the four directions, all things shine forth in radiant splendor."
Passing my days, how shall I repay your profound virtue? Amidst a grove of bamboo surrounding my bed, I propagate the ancestral style.

Entering the hall, he said: "With face yellowed and head white, I am a venerable Chan elder. I dwell upon the eastern ridges of Mount Ling. My mind is still, for I may observe the bright moon’s light;
My body is at leisure, so I am loath to encounter the world. High and low, dense and thick, there are thousands of bamboos, near and far...
Tens of thousands of pines fill the vast expanse; those that rise pierce the sky, while those that lean lie prostrate. Upon their aged branches, strength gathers in dense layers;
roots coil around strange rocks as dragons return to their caves. Their sound penetrates the long void as tigers roar in the wind. In years past, they were once employed by the Sovereign.
To this day, white clouds often seal it over.
A Memorial for the Reconstruction of Dajue Chan Temple at Xi-yu, composed by the Elder Duan of Xi-yu.
Striking coins for reconstruction—whether one gives them up is well, or whether one does not give them up is well; after a few more years, the fence [will stand].
The walls collapsed.
He addressed the assembly, calling out: "In this mountain monastery, the lecture hall is leaking and the quarters are crumbling.

For years there has been no donor to burn incense, and for many years few patrons have offered alms. I fear that there may be fellow practitioners from the ten directions or eminent travelers who might temporarily enter."
In the desolate mountains, it is difficult to establish a permanent residence; yet one may find joy in the streams and peaks, using pine and cypress for sustenance.

Fame and profit do not trouble the mind, nor does food and drink occupy one's thoughts. One ceases formal study under spiritual teachers and grows weary of visiting Zen monasteries; hearing the teachings is like the spring breeze.
Listening to talk of Chan is like recounting a dream. Dwelling together on the edge of the crags, we shared the same profound stillness. This is respectfully submitted.

Having returned from entering the city to seek alms in the early part of the Mid-Autumn month in the seventh year of Yuánfēng, I suddenly found myself pressed by the four elements [the physical body], and thus reflected upon my former vows.
He replaced the great pillars of the Treasure Hall and repaired the main gate of the Sangha Hall. His chests lacked even an inch of silk, and his bags contained no gold for medicine.
Unable to avoid entering the city to beg for alms, he knocked at every noble door; was there anyone who did not respond with joy?
Everyone was delighted everywhere, saying, "We have received the Elder’s visit in person.

Yet, when they offered five or ten coins and were immediately asked for a thousand cash or a hundred strings of cash, it was as if their very sinews were being pulled out. This is surely because my own merit and karmic conditions are shallow;
do not blame others. One knows for oneself that the hemp rope is short; why begrudge the depth of the bitter well? It is better to return early to the mountain crags and practice.
I am but a solitary recluse. Beholding the pure radiance of the moonlight, I gaze upon the solitary crane as my neighbor.
I vow to propagate Prajñāpāramitā and repay the Buddha’s profound kindness. I exhort all future descendants: do not beat such drums and pipes to disturb others.
A Verse on a Bountiful Year:
Do not take offense at this rustic old man’s idle talk. Lately, the Chan school has become multifaceted. First, one must understand the five houses and lineages;

thereafter, one should thoroughly study the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Lamp), the source of the patriarchs. Furthermore, one should discuss the various family records (*yulu*), transcribing them, carving woodblocks, and printing them.
Jian: "I read this from dawn until night; it is just like that of you, Dharma-brother. You must travel even further throughout the world until your two legs ache with exhaustion.
Upon entering the gate of a master, first examine the ancient precedents:

there was the wild shouting and reckless bellowing in the long corridors, and the clamorous chatter gathered in the Sangha hall. One can well imagine that on the path of Caoxi, there would be no one like [this]."
There are many such types. They further study four-six parallel prose and extensively read the poems of Zhuangzi and Laozi.

Regarding themselves as possessing refined elegance and graceful bearing, they seek to cultivate connections with officials for social advancement. As soon as they ascend the Dharma seat and lift their staff, they proclaim, "My very mind is Buddha," citing phrases that are utterly wondrous and profound.
Yet who among them has truly awakened to the ultimate principle? In the end, it is merely a matter of their own bellies.
This is utterly crude and reckless; it is to deny cause and effect. Such deluded ignorance will surely lead one to the side of demons.

With one's karmic consciousness in constant turmoil all day long, what year will there ever be for liberation? One races about with the arts of yin and yang, divination, medicine, acupuncture, and moxibustion, merely gathering up wares from the marketplace to sell.
It is all nothing but a desire for money, while further coveting favors, estates, and the patronage of the powerful and influential.
My younger brother Bianbian possesses some landed estates; he personally labors at the plowing and cultivation of his fields and gardens. Alas! The people of this world lack discernment;
they say that because he exerts his own physical strength and manages his affairs, he lacks the fortune and conditions [to be a monk].

Yet, when one gathers three hundred or five hundred disciples, their reputation moves the court nobles from afar, and they are recommended for the honor of the "Jin-yi" robe and the title of Master, receiving the imperial grace repeatedly.
These matters must be proclaimed. Who knows of Yaoshan? His assembly did not number more than ten. Zhaozhou’s meditation chair was originally missing half of it.
Deshan ate mud and earth; Yantou had no vinegar and no salt. Wuye declined three imperial summons, wandering freely and following conditions as they arose.
Had he been seen with his own eyes today, one would say he lacked both fortune and affinity. Thus does the rustic elder examine them.
Point! Great indeed is the boat traveling upon dry land! I have no other realization at present; I shall merely play the lion according to conditions.
The hair on its body is not made of thread; how could its head and tail be pulled by a rope? When looked upon, the thousand demons flee in terror;
when touched, the hundred beasts are left bewildered. This very skill remains on Vulture Peak, transmitted to people for ten thousand ages.
Xie Zhangting and Li Ba entered the mountains together in the intercalary fourth month of the fourth year of the Xiangshu era.
Amidst the mountain forests there was no heat; the clear breeze and bright moon cast a cool radiance.
The mountain streams flowed on and on without ceasing; white cranes cried out across the vast sky from amidst the clouds; and by the cliffs, fresh bamboo sprouted in the dew.
Gao Jie: At this time and in these sights, it is precisely the moment for sleep. Suddenly, I sensed someone pushing at my thatched gate. The mountain boy came out and asked who it was.
He reported, "The court official and Li Ba have come to tell me:
'The Sage is urgently summoning the Chief of the Secretariat and the Minister of Personnel to the Imperial Palace. I said to those two, 'They are truly like my Lion.'"
Displaying vigorous prowess, he emerges from his rocky cave; with a single roar, he brings forth an era of Great Peace. When the hundred beasts hear it, their brains shatter.
I urge you, sir, to serve the sagely and enlightened ruler with a public heart; do not harbor poisonous malice for the sake of private vengeance.

Regarding the worldly person’s four modes of conduct, I alone am most extraordinary. Having cast aside all the myriad anxieties of the human realm, I am utterly indifferent to wealth, honor, fame, and profit.
On the contrary, I reflect upon the Elder Śākyamuni, who did not know what was appropriate for people, yet instead commanded that one should [meditate] by day...
Cultivate wholesome dharmas at night; do not let the first and last watches of the night go to waste. During the middle watch, recite the sutras to regulate yourself.
Do not allow the conditions of sleep to cause this one life to pass in vain, resulting in nothing attained. If you were to instruct an old monk, I would have him see for himself:
atop the summit of Mount Ling, everyone lies down at once with a clod of earth as a pillow and falls fast asleep—suddenly!
When pulling him up, one must let him know that there is such a taste within sleep.
On the final day of winter in the year of Xīníng Yǐmǎo (1075), a chilling cold wind blew as thick snow fell. Beasts took refuge in crags and valleys; birds took refuge in...

Nesting in hollows, the elderly and the poor have nowhere to rest. They suffer through long nights, grieving over the passing months and years. Parents, wives, and children are each separated from one another.
Their hair is disheveled like that of ghosts; their flesh is withered and parched as if brushed with ink.

Their hands and feet are cracked and peeling, and they walk with great hardship, dripping fresh blood. Using a jar for a cauldron and grass for clothing, they lean on staffs, frail and feeble, speaking...
Choking with sobs, their cries are frequent, yet who will heed them? Often, out of ignorance, they are drenched with water.

It is said that because they did not cultivate themselves early in a previous life, they now lack food and clothing in this life. Birth does not arise, and death does not perish; I report this to the wise and the sagacious:
having failed to pay the taxes for the green sprouts and the corvée labor, they starve to death in the Yellow Springs—to whom can they speak?

One day, the Master went to the residence of Minister Zhang Gong. He was invited to a vegetarian feast, where the minister served him mutton dumplings to eat. After the Master had finished eating, the minister remarked, "What a trick!

The Master said, "I told you that beast was good to eat; it has run right into me. He then left behind this verse: The sheep’s head is a great treasure-trove; The sheep’s feet are a pair of jade pillars.
If you can eat them without chewing, You will see the Buddha within the Buddha.
In a year of drought, one prays for rain; on high mountains, it is good to plant fields. If eating vegetables allows one to become a Buddha, then even donkeys and horses would be reborn in heaven.
While you dwell at Mount Ling and are friends with Zhang Xianggong, I, Zhang Dun, invite you to visit my grave. Yet I eat only vegetarian food, while you eat meat.
On the birthday of Chancellor Zhang, the Master presented a white dog as a longevity offering.

In the mountains there were no sheep, so the dog served as a substitute for a sheep. Its head was without a double-tongue, its flesh was abundant, and its tail was long. It not only replenishes fatigue but also benefits the marrow;
at night, it offers something else worth contemplating.
The Master arrived at Pingjiang Prefecture. He received this verse from Chancellor Zhang:
"Eyes dim and ears deaf, my old self stands alone; In the forest depths there is no one, tears fall like pearls.
May you, Excellency, grant me rain from the clouds, To save the withered trees at the base of the sweet spring gully."
Seeing Master Ping off as he accompanies Chancellor Zhang to Tanzhou, his son comes to bid me farewell before departing for Tanzhou.
He wishes to see the Water Buffalo of Mount Gui; yet that buffalo’s horns have been there all along.
Upon seeing it at the crossroads, one should simply turn back and rest.
Lord Zhang was summoned to court; he declined on the grounds that his mother was elderly.
It is easy to transform iron into gold, but difficult to fulfill both loyalty and filial piety. Reflect upon this carefully:
how could it compare to the leisure of an old monk of no use beneath the green pines at Lingshan Gaoguan Chan Monastery in Changxing?
A Sacrificial Offering to the Late Minister of State, Zhang Yingqing.
On this day of the [month] year of the [year], I reverently take the universe as a vessel and the bright moon as an offering, and address the spirit of Minister Zhang, saying:

Having realized the fundamental true nature and ascended to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), you have attained the five blessings in full measure; your descendants shall hold the ranks of minister and general, their needs satisfied in every way.
Ten thousand feet. We humbly pray that you will partake.
Alas for Minister Zhang!
To be born is like a bubble arising upon the great ocean; to die is like a bubble submerging into the great ocean. Minister Zhang understood this; his words were pure.
"Worldly one! One dream has now passed through ninety springs.
When Chancellor Zhang was summoned to court and took his leave of the Master, the Master invited him into the abbot’s quarters.
After the tea and soup were finished, the Master said, "Please continue to protect and cherish the Buddha-dharma. The Chancellor replied, "I shall not..."
Xing did not abandon his devotion to protecting the Buddha-dharma. The Master ordered an attendant to fetch some sugar and give it to the official.

As the official was eating the sugar on the road, the Master asked, "Official, is it sweet? The official replied, "It is sweet. The Master said, "If it is sweet, then stay. The official laughed and then departed.
The Master subsequently entered the capital to pay his respects to Chancellor Zhang. The Chancellor’s wife was displeased and left behind this verse:
A single clap of thunder from above the heavens Passes over the old monk’s head. Fortunately, he is a man at ease; Why must he do such a thing?
The Master, at the request of Official Zhang, sang this "Zhuang" (Improvisation) on the offering of dumplings:
"Fragrant meat dumplings, plain vegetable dumplings— Served in full bowls, swallowed whole. Garbage passes right over the sandbar."
The dragon palaces and ocean treasuries are naturally clear and distinct.

Withdrawing from the pivot of state secrets at Mount Ling, you—intelligent, wise, upright, and honest—seeing that I am old and decrepit, have taught me to plant; now there are a thousand mulberry trees.
With ten billion pines and cypresses, I contemplate the ancestral teachings; they are most bitter, most bitter! Taking my leave, I return to the forest below to repay his kindness and virtue.
A Verse on Practicing Transformation at the Changfa Chan Monastery in Wukang, composed by the Elder Pòluò:
Wearing a tattered robe, dwelling in a dilapidated monastery, I have no afflictions. Borrowing a broken sedan chair, I go among the people.
The House. Tearing apart the cotton wadding and entrails, slowly searching for them.
Guest Prefect Lu (courtesy name: Menglao) invites [the host] to attend his official posting.
It is truly the blazing heat of the sixth month; deep within the white clouds, one sleeps at ease. Suddenly, a mountain boy comes to startle [the sleeper].
I replied: "The Old Man came from afar by boat to visit me by the streamside.
When he asked what words I had to say upon our parting, I spoke neither of teachings nor of Chan; I simply listened to the sound of governance.
It is like the water flowing before my mountain, returning to the vast sea—pure, clear, and eternally serene."

A Verse on Master Lu Ye’s Entry into the Mountains (with an appended verse on the Wild Old Man’s visit to the Master) Though wandering through this floating world brings no benefit, Master Pang delighted in transmitting the ancestral way. Having realized the essence of the school, there is nothing more to do;
I have bought a lute and purchased wine, yet I have not yet paid the money.
The old monk sits dazedly within the mountains. A fine friend from beyond the mundane world comes to visit me. That fine friend from beyond the mundane world suddenly descends the mountain;
I myself remain as before, sitting within the mountains.
To Imperial Censor Yu:
When the Son of Heaven is young and his ministers are young, governing the state and pacifying the people requires the deepest virtue.
I urge you to maintain a public mind and propagate the transformative influence of governance; this very mind is the mind of the Patriarch.
Accompanying various gentlemen on a journey through the mountains and waters of Meichang, my vigor has declined with the passing years; climbing hills and descending ridges, I pant like thunder.
Wild flowers and spring grasses fill the mountains in their splendor, while the calls of secluded birds urge me to turn back.

Presented to Assistant Minister Wu upon his entry into the mountains when a friend came to visit him at the firewood gate: The clouds and waters are vast and leisurely; the mountain streams and ravines are cold. Do not say that there is nothing to welcome you in this mountain home;
Let the ancient pines and tall bamboos be for your viewing as you please.

Apart from carefully examining the court, simply extinguish the fire within the mind; the path ahead will be level and smooth. With no snow or rain for three winters, each person may act as they see fit.
Invited by Lü Dàzī of Xuānchéng to visit Mount Huángbò.
In years past, Prime Minister Pei summoned Huangbo; today, Grand Chancellor Dai retains this old monk. You must know that this principle is neither of this age nor of antiquity;
like the single moon, it clearly illuminates the myriad streams.
Entering the Mountains with a Friend:

A Rhyme on Leisure At leisure, with nothing to do, I face the mountain screen; Ancient ravines and cold pines satisfy my rustic sentiments. In every place, the mountain flowers display their colors high and low;
From various kinds of hidden birds come sounds of coming and going.
Master Lü seeks the verse on sitting meditation;
Master Zhang delights in seeking immortality. Xu Liuzhu is like one carrying a wooden board: each sees but one side.
Prince Shu invited the Master to the capital.
Lord Jing requested that he lecture on Chan. A vegetarian feast was prepared at the Great Xiangguo Temple.

While they were reading the scriptures, Lord Jing entered the monastery; after the incense had been burned, he asked the assembly, "Before the Buddha appeared in the world, what sutras did they read?"
The assembly remained silent. The Master said, "When you gentlemen, Confucius and Mencius, had not yet appeared in the world, what books did you read? The official replied, "A clever monk.
The Master further said, "Namo Avalokiteśvara; he speaks forth all manner of dharmas, yet those of past and present remain submerged [in ignorance]."
Shengsheng was resentful toward the Bodhisattva.

One day, when Cai the Censor entered the mountains, he said, "Although your eye of the Way, Master, is clear, you would do well to go see Chan Master Fayong to refine your understanding of the causes and conditions of the past and present. The Master replied with a verse:

This rustic old man has been muddled throughout his life; his appearance is like that of a lacquer bucket. Upon inspection, he possesses no apertures at all, yet he still knows how to move his mouth for gruel and rice.
His speech is coarse and uncultivated; being dull and clumsy, he is incapable of serving others.

He himself knows his own eyes of wisdom are dim and that he does not understand the tangled complications of the Dharma. Suddenly, meeting a virtuous friend and a good companion, they urged me to go and consult Faryong.
I have heard that the Chan Master Fayong is highly esteemed by kings and ministers of great merit;

when he walks, his presence is majestic and resonant, and when he sits, he is surrounded by a thousand followers like gathering clouds. He wears fine brocade robes and eats delicacies, while his residence features carved beams and painted rafters.
An old rustic reflects upon this carefully: it is but a scene of worldly clamor and vanity.

Wandering the West Lake, I do not care for the elder Chan masters; they speak only of the highest of the high teachings. I do not care for the stream of those who lecture on the sutras; day after day they fan the pure breeze.
Yet I do love this West Lake, where beneath the Phoenix Bridge the waters flow eastward.
On my way to Xuanzhou at the request of Grand Councilor Lü Dàzī, I am departing for Xuancheng today.
The light of the moon illuminates the bamboo gate; on this journey, I have but a single robe, which I shall pull out and wear as the cold sets in.
On the heights of Lizang Pass, the plum blossoms have not yet faded; by the riverbank, the willow buds are lush and green. As we grasp hands at the parting ways, I cannot bear to leave;
yet what can be done? The spring breeze sends me back home.
In verse he replied:
"The Courtyard of Thorough Observation is empty beneath the trees; old, I grieve for myself alone. My kashaya robe serves as a makeshift raincoat. Upon Camel Bridge I gaze at the bright moon;
it is not for the sake of the plump tails of the *lúyú*."
The Master was at Huilin Monastery in the capital when he met Chan Master Yuanzhao. As Yuanzhao came out to meet him, he said, "A lion cub from the village!
and immediately assumed the posture of a lion. The Master responded with a verse on the spot:
"A lion cub from the village, playing in the village; His eyebrows and eyes move all at once. Opening his mouth, what is inside?"
Rough and uncouth. He does not care for people’s offerings; even if he were to perform his arts in the palace of an emperor, it would still be nothing more than a hollow clamor.
Furthermore, he composed a verse on Master Yuanzhao Chan:
The benevolent delight in the mountains; the wise delight in the waters. Bamboo, moonlight, pines, and wind are their constant companions.
Ceasing study and practicing non-action is my true teacher, dwelling amidst the white clouds upon a solitary peak in the depths.
The Master entered the city. When he met with the Provincial Governor, Li Chengyi, the latter remarked, "Since the Master is the pure Dharma-body, how is it that your head has turned white?
The Master replied, "This old monk has ten sorrows; because of these, my head has turned white."
He then sought out a brush and wrote:
"The First Sorrow: I am constantly afraid that the waters of the Yellow River will burst its banks and flow forth. Year after year, earth is piled up like mountains;
age after age, one must guard against the opening of the sack."
The second sorrow: when the waters of the rivers and lakes rise, it is truly difficult to remain. The regions of Su and Hu are all low-lying lands;
one must guard against floods submerging the fields.
The third sorrow: grain and rice are scarce among the people. Suddenly, after a day of famine, the poor will collapse from hunger.
One has nowhere to seek such a person.

This is the fourth sorrow. Look upon the Han Garden (the imperial academy); there are few among the literary peers. If the state wishes to employ men of talent, tears flow doubly as they find that neither poetry nor prose is matched by a mastery of the Classics.
The fifth sorrow: Ministers and officials pass down their vendettas from generation to generation; when will sons and grandsons ever bring this to an end?
I urge you, for the sake of the nation, to turn back early. The sixth sorrow:
Lately, generals and ministers are truly difficult to find. Sons and grandsons receive emoluments and prize gold, yet as soon as news of the frontier reaches them—
Frowning his brow, he expresses the seventh sorrow:
"The human world is vast, yet the old monk is filled with anxiety. Lately, temples have been converted into palaces and shrines;
the terraces, halls, bridges, and embankments of the state altars are being abandoned."

The eighth sorrow: The state’s extreme parsimony is my greatest anxiety; loyal ministers and filial sons will surely be hard to find, while petty men indulge in their own vanity and display their affectations.
The ninth sorrow: Lazy in supporting their parents, they seek to shave their heads; they plunder the people’s wealth to obtain ordination certificates, only to repay their past debts.
With eyes fixed in sorrowful longing, this is the tenth grief:
beneath the forest trees, where no one remains, twin tears flow. The Sage is far removed while false views draw near;
because of this, the wild elder has turned his hair white.
The Master observed that the floating world of wealth, honor, poverty, and low station all belongs to the realm of illusion and emptiness; yet people do not awaken to this.
He thus composed "Ten Verses on Emptiness" to warn the world:
Human life rarely fills a hundred years; A flower does not remain red for ten days. If you have wealth and do not practice giving, After death, it will all be a single void.
Clothing and food are all predetermined; follow conditions and accept one's fate until the end. Even if you were to strive mightily to acquire them, a sudden, untimely death would leave it all empty.

When wealth is abundant, it only turns into insufficiency; even with surpluses remaining, one still speaks of being destitute. Do not let your fortunes decline, for regret will leave everything empty.

Worldly affairs are as numerous as hemp and millet seeds; delusive thoughts arise in ever-increasing layers. With much greed, the mind is never satisfied; it is a total emptiness that results in loss. The physical body is not solid;
one constantly dwells in anxiety within this burning house. Failing to uphold and recite the Buddha’s sutras, one’s life passes idly into a state of total emptiness.

Not concerned with matters that do not concern oneself, one’s ears seem deaf when hearing the truth. Failing to understand the principle within one's own person, one idly manages a field of emptiness.
Bone and flesh are but temporarily gathered; wife and children are kept only to prevent their own deaths. When impermanence arrives all at once, this separation is but a field of emptiness.

While living at home, one was disrespectful; now that death has come, one vainly beats one’s breast. On the Cold Food Festival, one indulges in sightseeing and play; the ancestral offerings are but a hollow formality.
Wealth and status are abundant and sufficient—this is the merit sown by past causes. If one does not cultivate blessings in this life, the next world will be but a hollow void.
I urge you to share what remains in your home; repay the four debts of gratitude with depth. You must establish karmic connections early, lest you abandon them to a field of emptiness.
In response to Master Miao’an. (Attached is the verse by Master Miao’an):
"I have humbly observed that at Changfa Chan Monastery, there has never been a sight more rarely encountered than these few dilapidated and leaking corridors. One...
The ancient hall that once stood there has collapsed; it cannot withstand the rain, snow, wind, and frost, and its structure is now entirely dilapidated.

The rafters and bamboo mats are hollowed out, and the incense burners have forever ceased to emit smoke. Upon the scripture stands, there are no longer any scrolls. Looking at this solitary village, one cannot help but feel deep lamentation.
Furthermore, there are no eminent disciples from distant lands to serve as attendants; let the local lay followers provide whatever offerings they find convenient.
They compete to amass wealth, yet they do not apply their minds to building [meritorious works]. Their estates serve only as provisions for sustenance;

when the silkworms mature, each harvests silk and gauze, yet even for vegetarian offerings there is no oil or salt, and it is difficult to find milk or flour for meals. Every day, jackals and wolves form packs.
The donor has never set eyes on him; when Zen travelers from the ten directions arrive, how could they not feel revulsion?
Where can he find a place to settle his body? With a single turn of his feet, he traverses them all at once. Piteous is this venerable elder monk; his dwelling here was not by his own will.
It was surely not for the sake of propagating the Buddha-dharma, nor out of lingering attachment to fame and profit. Rather, it was due to a forced...
To follow human sentiment and swallow this withered austerity for a mere moment is not as good as bidding farewell and returning home early.

There is no need to labor over transforming this place; mountain dwelling remains ever tranquil and spacious. Furthermore, there is not even half a tile to be found at my gate. How many Zen groves exist throughout all quarters? Yet none of them are fit to be recommended over this.
I respectfully address the local magistrate and patrons: you are merely exhausting yourselves in vain training for the sake of the Patriarchs.

I have instructed several village monks; for now, I shall manage my own affairs and prepare my own meals. There is no need to further engage in the ten directions, lest one see the state and its counties troubled by such matters.
I have briefly written these few lines in a poetic style, all of which are sincere exhortations.
I, the mindless old rustic of the Great Song, do not understand the entanglements of Chan and the Way.

Unwilling to dwell in places of excellence, I maintain myself in a ruined monastery according to circumstances. Suddenly, accompanying the abbot into the city, we happened upon Wu Kang seeking us out.

The old rustic was unwilling to accept the responsibility, but the abbot urged him, saying it would be well. Accepting the invitation, we entered the mountains together; he laughed at me for having accepted such a withered existence.
Sent by official business to Fengci, the village elder followed his circumstances and composed ten verses on the "Ten Excellences" in response.
The First Excellence: Layer upon layer of emerald peaks—where can they be sought? Dragons coil and tigers turn; few know this place. It cannot be captured in painting, for it is not a human creation.
The second excellence: A secluded pine gate opens onto the great road; the wooden barrier remains unbarred, cutting off the clamor of the world.
Flakes of white cloud arrive from time to time. The third excellence:
Let the dust be swept away as it pleases by the wind. The white ox follows its steps past the crags, eating all at once.
The grass by the roadside has been cleared away—this is the fourth excellence. A frosty monkey suddenly arrives from within the forest; at the dead of night, it lets out a single cry upon the ridge.
The bright moon in the heavens shines forth as the clouds part.
The fifth excellence: Swifts and sparrows do not come to clamor beneath the forest trees; from time to time, an old crane rests upon a lofty pine, its clear cry startling a hundred birds.
The sixth excellence: Dry firewood and soft rice from the mountain fields; though there be no hundred flavors or rare delicacies, the gruel and rice are served as they come.
The conditions are favorable for advancing on the Path;

this is the seventh delight. With clear moonlight shining over the front and back streams, I sit in stillness deep into the night, contemplating the fleeting nature of life. I have finished reciting the seven fascicles of the Lotus Sutra, every sound brought to completion.

The eighth excellence: When people meet one another, there is nothing to say; they simply wish for each year to be stronger than the last, and that the delivery of grain taxes to the government may be prompt.

The ninth excellence: Before the gate, an ancient stream grows duckweed and pondweed; medicinal herbs are planted in succession to provide for the four seasons. This is the forest of guarding poverty.
Below, there are no afflictions.
This is the tenth excellence: for now, even mosquitoes do not come to disturb one. As the pine wind blows through the flutes, its sound resonates through the vast sky;
truly, this is where a mountain monk may dwell to grow old.
The Announcement for the Construction of the Wheel Treasury at Jiekong Monastery on Mount Wu:
This revolving scripture treasury was established by the Great Being Maitreya.

Observing that sentient beings of the末代 (final age) are indolent and lax, unable to recite scriptures, practice seated meditation, or cultivate according to the Dharma, he created this excellent cause so that it may pervade the entire realm of *sāhasra-lokadhātu*.
To continue the Buddha’s life-force of wisdom so that it shall not be severed, the mountain monk Changzhi has exerted every effort to solicit a patron and establish this auspicious connection.

When the patron enters the mountain to offer their wealth, they should maintain a mind of sincere reverence, vowing that in a future age at the three assemblies under the Dragon Flower Tree, they may gather in one place together with all those of superior virtue.
Written on the day of the sixth month in the year of Kaimei (1103) during the Chongning era. Old [man].
The Monk’s Letter.
The Master built a small hermitage beside the temple and named it Guiyun (Returning Clouds). He would frequently write verses and poems upon its walls, saying:

In my old age, I nurture my idle body beneath the forest trees; The thatched cottage is pure and empty, where not even a mosquito or gnat is found. From where does the pine-wind arise along the single path?
It enters the pines and pierces through the bamboo at two or three spots.
Rising from sleep, the stone pillow and wicker bed are low upon the single mat; having awakened, the sun has already set in the west.
Turning over within a mass of white clouds, a single strain of fisherman’s song lingers by the emerald stream.

Beholding the pine, a fragment of cloud suddenly rises and departs; the aged crane soars once more on high. Only the ancient pine tree before the crag remains—its green, long-reaching branches endure through the cold of winter.
Basking in the warmth by a thatched cottage facing south—when the weather is cold, basking in the sun is best; the great orb surpasses a gentle fire, for it is first and foremost free of smoke.
Written playfully in twenty-three characters.
Who would have known that the myriad phenomena are impermanent? Beneath the forest trees, the leisurely man is himself busy. I recall the eminent monk who maintained his solitary integrity;
how shameful, this old age and illness!
One cannot recite the sutras, nor can one practice seated meditation. One eats but a single meal at midday; when weary, one stretches out the legs and sleeps.
When the time comes, one simply goes forth without fetters. Let the Eastern Sea turn into mulberry fields as it may.
I describe myself and lament my solitary old age. Now seventy-three years of age, I have not plowed a single plot of field, nor raised a single cocoon of silkworms.
My belly has never known hunger; before the cold sets in, I have clothing to cover me. Having fortunately encountered a time of great peace, I cannot yet bid farewell to this world.

Furthermore, I describe how this mountain monk, wandering aimlessly, dwells in seclusion among the crags. Sitting in stillness, he uprightly unrolls the books of the ancient sages; he loves nothing more than the moon shining upon the pines and bamboo.
Long have I not donned purple or crimson robes nor worn the golden fish insignia;
I dwell in seclusion by the crags, my only shelter a thatched hut. Here, the pure breeze dispels the summer heat, and in this solitude, few harbor greedy desires.
In the deep stillness, the cries of birds break the silence; in meditation, no monk comes to inquire. After the midday meal, I descend into the forest; flower-rain falls in profusion.

Having woken from sleep, I am too weary to move my feet; as the sun sets, the shadows gather upon the pine bower. All myriad sounds fall silent in vast solitude; I hear only the calls of the mountain birds.
Sitting dully like one who is insane—only then can one be called a true renunciant. A solitary monkey departs beyond the heavens; a hundred birds do not offer flowers.

In the deep mountains at night, the birds have ceased their cries; only the cranes call out as they soar toward heaven. The wild elder’s hair and bones grow cold; hearing their sound, he cannot sleep.
The embers in the brazier are like water; in this solitude, few people know. Old and worn, I cannot find rest at this freezing midnight hour.
My eyes grow dim and I find it hard to distinguish characters; my ears are deaf and I do not hear sounds. Sitting by a cliff in the stillness of night, I see the moon but not the stars.

The mundane and the sacred do not share the same destination; the Buddhas and Patriarchs do not follow the same path. A person who is free and unencumbered should laugh at the picking up of blossoms and weeds.

Mountain Dwelling Poem By an ancient temple at Mount Wu, near the edge of a stream, The lofty pavilion and empty hall reveal the fullness of the scene. In the forest’s solitude, the hearth fires have long been extinguished;
Yet before sleep, one still hears the sound of night-faring boats.

At seven years old I dwelt in the mountains; now I am seventy. The mountain’s radiance and the pines and bamboos press upon one with a chilling cold. Deep in the night the fire is extinguished and the hearth-ashes grow cold;
a paper quilt enfolds my body like a mass of white snow.
At the ancient temple on Mount Wu, cold pines stand straight; An old crane makes its nest at the very summit.
I love only the sound of its clear cry after midnight, When the moon is bright and the sorrow fills the mountains.
The pines and bamboos are lush green by the deep ancient stream; I have thatched a cottage and named it Returning Clouds.
Since I began my travels among officials and bureaucrats, this rustic elder has had no desire to see men of high station.
I laugh at myself as my years grow old and snow fills my hair; let winter, summer, and spring and autumn come as they may. In the solitude of the forest, what is there to find joy in?
The mountain birds sing of their own accord, and the spring flows on its own.
I perceive myself as old and of no further use; poets mock me in wonder and commoners sneer at me. My eyes grow dim and my ears dull, and I lack the mental strength;
whether something is right or wrong, I know nothing of it.
Old, I detest the arrival of worldly guests; alone I drift upon a solitary boat to roam the stream. Lodging by night among the reeds, I admire the bright moon;
surely no idle matters weigh upon my heart.
In old age, with nothing to do, I close my wooden gate. Leisurely beneath the trees, what is there to be done? Do not say that this thatched hut has nothing within;
before the window, flakes of white clouds drift by.
Decrepit and frail, I do not descend from the mountain; I dwell in a hermitage among crags and valleys, seated amidst the woods. The moonlight enters my chamber, illuminating it from time to time;
the cries of solitary birds are heard, and all is even more tranquil.
The rustic elder rejoices, yielding freely to nature. With nothing to do after his midday meal, he enjoys the forest and springs. No one comes to his gate all day long;
at night, he faces the lofty pines while the moon hangs in the sky.

In old age, my spirit awakens and becomes even clearer; deep in the night within my secluded chamber, I recite the Lotus Sutra. My children and grandchildren must surely grow weary of me as they sleep;
thus, I strike the stone chime four or five times from time to time.
This old rustic is too lazy to accompany worldly guests; he sits in stillness within his thatched hall and sleeps in peace. Do not say there is no one to attend to you amidst the woods;
pines, bamboos, streams, and mountains are right before your eyes.
In my old age, I find joy in having no affairs; when I sit at leisure, my thoughts grow light. Beyond this single body there is nothing else;
the autumn waters are clear and the night moon is bright.
My eyes grow dim and my ears deaf; what is the cause of this? Who can explain this matter for me?
With no one to enjoy the company of beneath the forest trees, when weary, I lean alone against an ancient pine and sleep.
With nothing to do, my heart is joyful as I grow old; I cultivate my nature in the mountains to pass these remaining years. For years no one has come from the four quarters;
at my gate, perpetual day is but twilight.
Before the cliff stand two or three pine and bamboo trees; scorched by the sun and buffeted by the wind, they gradually wither.
Though their fallen leaves lie scattered everywhere and no one sweeps them away, their pure sound still resonates from dawn until dusk.
Human affairs drift on endlessly; I am too weary to climb them further. I sit in stillness within my thatched cottage amidst the white clouds. At night, I gaze upon the bright moon as my lofty lamp;
its single path of pure light illuminates ten thousand mountains.
Observing the willows casting their green eyes downward, I first realize that spring has arrived in the human world.
Gazing afar at the Southern Mountains where the snow has completely melted, a single branch of cold plum remains in bloom.
The water is clear, the mountain colors reflect against the blue sky; Sitting quietly in my thatched hall, I have no desire to sleep. I delight in gazing at the pines atop the crags and the moon;
Then I hear once more the cry of a cicada from a tall willow tree.
Deaf, he does not hear the drums atop the tower; blind, he can hardly see the midnight lamp.
After the sound of a single song by a fisherman has faded, the returning clouds drift freely and boundlessly across the heavens.
Unaware that the day has passed, I sit in silence within my hermitage. Wild birds fly away without carrying off even a flower;
there are only white clouds coming to keep me company.
Reverend Kōchi’s discourse on the three objects of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* reflects the compassionate, grandmotherly heart of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
These inherent virtues (*dharmatā-guṇa*) are established by others as mere names; they are like the cold plum blossoms atop the ridge, already bearing spring.
Snow. For nine years he faced the wall, toiling his own form.
To cultivate virtue, who would mix mercury with gold? The myriad phenomena and the forest of existence are not yet many; even such vastness must arise from the earth.
Arise! There is no way to avoid the heavens;
the Virtuous One entered the sea to seek pearls, going deeper and deeper for mani-jewels, various treasures, and gold. Today, he has brought his reward to the Persian King.
The Way: Do not sell glass to others.

This verse summarizes the transformation of his cultivation of nature (*xing*) as well as the general and the particular. All deliberation is but the moon at the edge of the sky; everyone’s discourse is but a single scene.

"Emptiness! Each person must sweep the snow from their own doorstep and listen to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*’s 'Sevenfold Investigation of the Mind' and 'Eightfold Analysis of Vision. With this verse, I present it to my teacher."
The Master of this lecture said: "You should have attained the Dharma through Chan;
yet when the mind was sought at the seven locations, the search failed. Stupefied Ānanda did not awaken to the ground of reality.
To insist on seeking until one attains a 'seeing without mind' is merely washing clods of earth in the mud."
The teaching of the "Eight Returns" has been transmitted for a long time; since antiquity, its various lineages have each branched out.
Even if one were to reach the time of non-returning, it would still be like a shrimp leaping but unable to escape the measuring basket.
Another version says:
"Bending and twisting like a door hook; each time it is picked up, there is one more sorrow. It is better to become a Chan practitioner:
practice until you reach the state of no-mind, and then simply rest."
*Sūmòzhē*: Encountering years of famine, this is seen everywhere; among them, this year’s floods have submerged everything. Parents and children are separated, with nothing left to cherish.
I hope for the wealthy and noble to come to our rescue. The farmers are most pitiable; how can one bear to see the monks of the ancient temple [in such distress]?
Lin [the Master] translated this as "The Hall of Compassionate Fields. Day and night he burned incense and offered frequent prayers: "May the Yellow Heaven protect and provide skillful means!
'Ox-song, ox, ox, ox—rest, rest, rest! Do not pull the plow or drag the harrow anymore; let it be as you wish through winter, summer, autumn, and spring, without a rope."
Without a rope, without a standard, and without a hook—this morning it was released toward the desolate burial mounds; in the vast and profound darkness, let it simply rest.
The song of the wooden fish is originally from the trees beneath the deep forest; bent and contorted, it hides its form within the secluded valley, only to be felled by a clever craftsman.
Come! They force me to carve out my eyes and hang me before the hall as a "fish-drum," making me cry out with every sound for the sake of the multitude's suffering.
Upon the long platform bed, I sleep clutching a blade; the fire-sticks strike my belly from time to time.
Being a fish of such high station, I am hung upon the red beam atop a precipitous cliff. Let me roam freely across the five lakes and four seas—who fears the dragon?
A dot is placed upon the forehead at the gate.
In the Song of the Twelve Hours, it is dawn at the hour of Yin:
the crows and birds cry out incessantly; the eyes have opened, yet one is still too lazy to rise, turning over once more upon the bed.
The sun rises at the hour of Mao (5–7 a.m.). Having put on one's robes and finished washing the face, one drinks a bowl of congee until it is gone.
One continues until the time for the midday meal, eating until full. At the hour of the meal, even a fierce fire requires no fuel. One *sheng* is ten *he*; eight *liang* is half a *jin*.
The sun has not yet set; the kettle of hot water is always boiling. If no idle guests come, it is time for a good nap.
At the hour of Shun (the seventh watch), lifting my head, I see not a single kinsman. Among the peach and plum pits of a thousand years, what person of former times can one seek?
The sun sets at You (the seventh hour). No one arrives at the gate; within the house, all is leisurely and carefree. Who could possibly run about outside?
At Huanghun (the eighth hour), the rat emerges from its burrow. Clapping hands, one tries to drive it away, but it cannot be stopped; they screech and squeak as they call out to one another.
The hour of Ren-ding (Hai) has arrived; it is not that I am particularly indolent. Having removed my shoes, I lie upon my bed to sleep, with nothing left to anticipate.
At the hour of Zhong-yè (Zi), I sleep most perfectly and pleasantly; though I have had a dream, to whom can I tell it?
At the hour of Chou (1–3 a.m.), the waning moon shines upon the doors and windows. On the tower above, the cock crows at dawn; the sky is cold as the Great Dipper turns.
At the hour of Si (7–9 a.m.), there is no fixed limit to one’s meals; the soup and vegetables lack salt and vinegar, and one usually eats but a little.
At noon in the land of the southern sun, with both hands I rub and press my belly. My trousers are worn through at the knees; who else is there to find to mend them?

The Dharma-grandson Bhikṣu Shijiao recompiled the "Words of the Fisherman.
Whenever the Master sat watching the bright moon and sang these "Words of the Fisherman," people delighted in hearing his voice; there were none who did not hasten toward him in great numbers.
They arrived, all of them joyfully forgetting to return.
As the constellations shifted and the stars moved, the sky gradually grew light. Suddenly, they heard the cries of pelicans; the mountain temple bells rang out as the crowd surged.
The wooden fish gongs clamored as the ferry boat crossed to the shore and the officials set off upon the main road.
The light boat races once more upon the Long River to seek its prey; I add fresh fragrant bait to my hook. Having caught the scaled dragon, it leaps within the boat.
Hehe! I laugh; how wonderful the life of a fisherman is throughout the world!
The waves are stilled at West Creek, clear as a silken brocade. A single sail is hoisted high, riding the favorable wind. Only then does a thin line appear across the heart of the waves;

*Admonition for the World*
I see that the people of this world are deluded, even more so; they do not record the time of the eighth year of Xining. Today, when rice is cheap, they have no sense of shame;
they eat fish and meat in the morning and grow fat on lard by evening. On the roads, there are countless skulls; when one person devours another, who is it?
Within the six realms of rebirth, beings wander on their own accord; each person in the world seeks only their own advantage.
Furthermore:
The village elder shares his concerns with you: there are three axes in this world—greed for wealth, and lust for wine and beauty—which do not know rest until old age.
They destroy human life and reduce one to a parched skull. Suddenly, when the four elements fall ill, one lies upon the bed with a vacant gaze.
The hair upon your head is black as lacquer, yet you have never cultivated your mind and conduct. I urge you to awaken early; do not wait until the rain drenches your head.
I see many people reciting the Buddha’s name whose mouths are sweet but whose hearts are bitter; their bellies are full of snakes, and their anger is like a fierce tiger.

In vain you have read the Tripitaka; reciting the Buddha's name with such [a mind] is mere idle talk. If the mouth is virtuous but the heart is impure, there will be no response to the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
When one insight illuminates the four directions, the mind becomes like a celestial jewel mirror.
I exhort you to study;
through study one becomes a sage. Without study, one remains an ordinary person. The sage is noble and the ordinary person is base, yet the worthy one lies between them.
The spring days are warm and the birds warble their songs; time is precious—how could one dare to remain idle?

through vast eons one cannot escape. Rebirth and death appear and disappear again and again, solely because of worldly attachments; lacking the conditions to give rise to the sun of wisdom, morning and evening pass without realization.
Its functioning is like glue and lacquer—this very thing is shown to all people: it is neither empty nor real.

Gradually awakening to the clear and harmonious days of the fourth month, a single sound of the pure gong resonates through the mountains and rivers.
With a mind lucid and breath refreshed, free from all constraints, I am left with this noble man to accompany me in night meditation.
Xie Zimei has long lived in seclusion, entering the mountains knowing herself to lack both merit and affinity.
An old woman sleeping by day in a thatched hut—today Qianmei comes from afar to visit me.
You have no "this" (money), and I have no Chan.
The Master’s livelihood is poor, yet his lofty discourse and eloquence are treasures of pearls. One truly knows that he has attained the principle of non-birth;
he gladly serves as a man beneath the trees in the Cloud Hall.
The Layman Wang visited Master Zhengbao Ben.
The Layman Wang applied himself with diligence to his practice: "Do not linger over a drop of water from Caoxi; it is difficult to encounter the blue-eyed barbarian monk."
Do not scheme for trifles and chatter incessantly. Easy it is, yet difficult it is. To the east flows the water of the Xia River, curving around the peaks of Mount Bian.
At the meeting place before the Summer-Dispelling Tower, one faces the clear breeze, the bright moon, the stream, and the mountains.
The Layman Zhang came to visit;
the Layman of Qinghe has not been seen for many years. A smile at our meeting confirms that we truly share a karmic affinity. Do not be surprised that this old monk has no special words to say:
the ordinary mind is the Zen of the Patriarchs.
On the Lantern Festival of the Guiwei year of the Chongning era, drifting clouds had dispersed and the moon hung at the edge of the sky. A single path of pure light illuminated the Xi River;
face-to-face, it was presented—there were no words to be spoken.
The lay practitioner Shen Deqing visited me to seek out the traces of Master Yao.

The moon shines upon the cold pines, their green needles glistening; frost gathers on the emerald bamboos, revealing their variegated patterns. Yet when I gaze at the reflection in the hall, my regret lies in not beholding his living countenance.

the ancestral Way has long been obscured, and the branch of Linji was broken; today it suddenly flourishes once more, eclipsing the moon over the Shaoxi River.
A Gift for Elder Huī: In the past you were Old Man Wulong; now you dwell at Nandong. You have cut off Linji’s Chan and pierced through Yunmen’s path.
To instruct those traveling monks: when the time comes, you must realize it; do not be muddled. The bitter gourd is uniquely sweet; the sweet melon is uniquely... [bitter].
Suffering! To meet face-to-face is already halfway there. Do not speak of Heyshan’s ability to beat the drum;
the ninth day of the ninth month is Double Ninth, and the fifth day of the fifth month is Dragon Boat Festival.
The disciple has long wandered through the world for many years, nurturing his fledglings beneath the forest trees. Today, together with the clouds, he soars beyond the mundane;
perched high atop an ancient pine on a mountain peak, he lets out a single clear cry that all under heaven shall know.
Master Sun Dao Yue traveled to various quarters;
the autumn wind blows and yellow leaves fall. Like the moon emerging from a mountain gate, it illuminates the vast sky without obstruction;
a solitary cloud and a lone crane are well-suited to rely upon one another.
A pack of descendants can do nothing; as soon as they are gathered, they are sent out into the misty thickets. Do not be surprised that thorns grow upon the level plains;
they rise straight up as great waves from the vast blue sea.
The Master’s disciple, Sōng-ri, a wanderer, now wishes to go toward the mountain ahead. For now, he shall proceed by asking for the way before the mountain.
If one encounters a donkey or a horse at the foot of the mountain, among the small branches, there must surely be one that flourishes.
My household affairs have no fixed source; though I tell my descendants, they refuse to rest. Today I release them to the Master to go forth;
once they enter the gate, I must ensure they immediately show their heads.
Hearing of the auspicious scenery of Xiangjing, I have built a thatched hermitage;
I love the auspicious scenery of Xiangjing. Its transcendent character and style are unique: my body does not mingle with the mundane world, while my mind may be joined with the bright moon.
I have recently heard that you have built a thatched hermitage; why did you not tell me? On the outside, the foundation must be firm; within, it must be perfectly complete.
Trim the thatch into a flat top; plant bamboo with high joints. Pound the hemp fibers, mix them with lime and charcoal, and once dry, it will be as hard as iron.
In winter, it is naturally warm; in the summer months, there is no scorching heat. For an old man whose hair and bones shiver with cold, dwelling here wards off the wind and snow.
There is no need for great effort; striving for cleverness often results in clumsiness.
Presented on the final winter festival of the season of Xingning to Xiangjing Xiushi Zhengxi.

Sitting by the fire in a thatched hut, lingering as the sun rose, I was unaware that the cock had crowed.

Floating life upon my pillow has passed half a century; my short hair is wispy and white as frost. On the banks of West Creek lies the mountain of my former home;
