Master Yunfeng has come to visit.
In throngs of three by threes and two by twos, they chatter in clusters; when has the lion ever feared the tiger?
Even were the Snowy Mountains ten thousand fathoms high, once the great sun shines upon them, they leave no trace behind.
Traveling with fellow monks to Mount Jinshan and Zhanggong Cave, white clouds suddenly arose as we reached Longyou.
Though the immortal cave is deep, how could I not linger? Today I have returned once more to the side of my former cliff;
among the travelers, there is none whose head is not drenched by the rain.
Expressing My Feelings:
Retreating from View to Return to the Mountain Clefts Living in seclusion, visitors are rare; I sleep soundly upon my high and tranquil couch. Cane in hand, I wander around my thorn-bush gate;
Far removed from fame and profit, I am able to forget both right and wrong. Pine winds dispel the thinness of summer heat; Mountain moonlight illuminates the faint glow of fireflies.

Brewing tea, the bowl overflows with snow; scooping spring water, half my robe is dampened. The clouds’ intent is dense, whether in adversity or success; in the end, it differs from that of worldly men.
Recalling the Lotus Peak community, I think only of the wonders of Mount Huading. Who would be willing to turn their head back and penetrate deeply into the wondrous, profound mystery?
A Letter of Thanks for the Gift of Flour Amidst the Snow The spring snow covers the crags and valleys;
within these mountains there is nothing at all. Having received the gift of flour amidst the snow, I am still short by ten catties of bran.

Thanking Someone for Gifting Charcoal from the Mountains and a Firebrand: The smoke has caused tears to flow. Having received the charcoal gifted amidst the snow, I pray that you may excel day by day.
Presented to Xiao Wang, the Young Scholar.
A single seedling from the Southern Mountain is planted in the earth; in days to come, it shall become a hundred-foot pine.
If it should meet with wind and clouds, its form will gradually ascend and reveal itself as a dragon.

The tea is refined and elegant; its brewing surpasses even imperial offerings. As the incense smoke from the burner burns auspicious blossoms, how many fine clouds of leaves are there? They float long and light like falling snow.

With the "crab-eye" bubbles rising in fresh abundance, the pure sweetness washes away the drowsiness of the spirit. My withered bowels can withstand but three cups; yet even so, my dreams and soul feel somewhat refreshed.
Entrusting this to Luo Dao to seek out the Elder Duanyu and convey these words to him:
"I am looking for Duanyu to escort the Elder. If you can relinquish your waiting, I shall be delighted;
there is no need to search elsewhere."

When Layman Wu looked at a Chan manual, the Wild Old Man said, "An old rustic has come to your home and sees you looking at a Chan manual. You must exert your own mental faculties; do not be intimidated by the Patriarchs."
The Three Teachings—Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism—are honored as supreme. Their profound kindness is such that we feel shame; our misfortunes have even reached our descendants.
Master Shang’an is ill.
The four snakes suddenly cause turmoil; the thread within the box is no longer orderly. The ancient master beneath the forest trees goes or stays according to his own convenience.

Lacking the power to perform a somersault, there is fundamentally neither clarity nor dullness. Clarity and dullness depend solely upon the mind. Although there is no calculating in daily life, one must investigate with careful scrutiny.
Shown to the two disciples Jian and Er while ill:

The mountains of Wushan stretch toward Mount Tianmu; The mountain colors are ever-constant in their green, the waters ever-constant in their clarity. The radiance of the mountains and the hues of the waters flow together;
From patriarch to patriarch, from lamp to lamp, they continue in succession.
In this testament to his disciple Wenhui, he says:
"I have lived a life of complete sufficiency. Throughout my entire life, I have possessed nothing; as soon as I die, I shall be buried. Do not fall into worldly custom.
This is the true eulogy.
Forty-seven transmissions completed; divine light is revealed as an illusory form. From the beginning, to whom has the Way been explained?
Donning the straw raincoat, one laughs at oneself—Vimalakīrti. Ehi! (Aha!)
Every tree has its bark; every person has their face. Transmitted upon paper, it is a double case.
From antiquity to the present day, how can one see it thus? What a fine painter! He does not transmit the dead man.
*The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wushan Duan of Huzhou*, Volume Lower.
The Biography of Chan Master Xi Yu Duan, composed by the Shramana Shi Dehong of Gaoyang.
As for Master Duanzi, he was a native of Wuxing. Initially, upon seeing a man performing with a lion, he attained enlightenment regarding the essential point of the mind. Thus, [the record begins].
His brocade robes were like his skin; he wore them from time to time and thus took them as his moniker.
He resided at Xiyu Mountain, succeeding Chan Master Yue of Cui Feng in Gusu. Since Xiyu was close to Huzhou, he would often enter the city wearing his brocade robes during snowfall.
Children clamored and pursued him, begging for money from passersby; as soon as he received it, he distributed it to those suffering from hunger and cold.

When Qian Mumu was traveling to his official post in eastern Zhejiang, he encountered him there and invited him to a meal the following day. On the morning of the appointed day, Fandu went alone; seeking shelter from the rain, he entered a house by the roadside.
A young woman came out to greet him, but shortly her husband arrived and scolded him, driving him away. Ultimately, Fandu was arrested by the patrol guards. Qian Mumu [heard of this].

The official hurried the guest along. Upon seeing him, he asked for the reason. The guest replied, "I have come to deliver word to Master Qian that I was originally heading to a vegetarian feast, but a matter of illicit passion arose on the way;
please allow me to eat my fill. When Mu Fu heard this, he was both startled and amused. He looked at the guest and said, "This monk has not a single speck of suspicion in his breast.
Furthermore, he once saw the man carrying a dead chicken while walking briskly. Mu Fu pulled at his robe and asked where he was going. The man replied: [as above].
The rooster had been harmed by a wildcat; according to the law, it was not permitted to be eaten. [The owner] intended to discard it in the water, but Zhiduàn earnestly sought it back.
As people gathered along the road to watch, he chanted: "I shall give you this only if you can provide a verse. Zhiduàn knelt and composed a memorial text, saying:

"As for this spirit, while alive it suffered the calamity of hawks and crows; upon death, it faces the disaster of boiling cauldrons. While alive, it required you to announce the dawn; after death, there is no one to collect and bury it."

He said, "I dedicate this to transform the donor; I give my own belly to serve as your coffin" (one version says: "The *ācārya* had nothing else to offer, so he gave his belly to serve as your coffin").

Having finished speaking, he took the chicken and left it for those who were hungry. Because he was able to recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, people from Hu-lake vied with one another to invite him.
He would certainly obtain five hundred coins; then, opening the volume, he would recite a few lines and immediately take the money, sitting on the ground before departing.

Those who were deficient or coarse he would replace with others and leave. He was fond of singing the "Fisherman's Song" (*Yùfǔ cí*), which he invariably sang on moonlit nights until dawn. There was a mad monk who [accompanied him].
He was known as Master Touhou. Using heterodox ways, he incited the common folk; even the scholar-officials were complacent with his delusions.
While he was facing off against Governor Lü of Danyang over a meal of meat, Xuedou went straight up to him and pointed, saying, "At this very moment, what is Buddha?
Touhou could not immediately respond. Xuedou struck him on the head and pushed him over before departing. There was also another sorcerer.
His name was Butuo (Not Relying). Outside the city walls of Xiuzhou, there was a Buddha image upon which a pagoda had been built;

the entire city held it in faith and reverence. Butuo saw this and pointed his staff at it, saying, "What is the Buddha? Before Butuo could even deliberate on a response, Duan kicked it over and departed.
Chancellor Zhang Zihou requested him to ascend the seat and commissioned Yu Xiulao to compose a memorial inscription describing the event, which said: "Pushing it over and turning back."
He kicked over his footrest without leaning on it. Before he had even recited the seven-fascicle Lotus Sutra, he heard the sound of the "Fisherman" chant once.
When the *śramaṇa* official reached this point in the recitation, Zhiyuan stopped him with a wave of his hand and said, "Stop. He then sat down and chanted in a drawn-out melody:
"I am originally a lone fisherman of Xiao and Xiang; I go east and west, north and south. The assembly praised him in unison, and Zhiyuan looked at them and smiled.
He said, "I observe the Dharma of the Dharma-King; such is the Dharma of the Dharma-King. He then descended from his seat. Zithou invited him to stay for a meal.
Duan, speaking with indignation, recited a verse: "Zhang Dun, Zhang Dun! You ask me to visit your grave, Yet I eat only vegetarian food, While you consume meat.
Zithou laughed heartily. At that time, Lü Taewei Jifu was also staying in Danyang. The three men would pass the day together, following Jifu.
I have just recited the merits of *dhyāna-samādhi*, which is said to be the foremost among all the *prajñās*.

Huiqing practiced it for ten years, yet Zithou alone praised it, saying, "Forging [it] can dispel sorrow. Ji Kang attained immortality, yet in the end he died by the "sword-release" (*jianjie*). Duan spoke a verse, saying: "Master Zhang loved to study immortality;
Master Lü loved to practice seated meditation. Xu Liu compared them to roof-boards: Each saw only one side. [Thus I] heard.
These [stories] have been transmitted as objects of amusement. At the beginning of the Yuanyou era, Chan Master Yuanzhao retired from Huilin Temple in the capital and returned to Gusu.
Upon seeing Dan at Ganlu Temple, he asked, "Are you not Dan Shizi?
Dan replied, "I am. Yuanzhao teased him, saying, "You are merely a village lion. Dan responded instantly, "A village lion is played with in the village; its eyebrows and..."
His eyes moved all at once; he opened his mouth and belly, acting with utter simplicity and disregard for human service.
Even if one were to bring him to the palace of an emperor, it would still be nothing more than a hollow clamor. Yuanzhao was pure and refined, yet he did not realize this was a mockery.
Duanke was traveling from Wuxi and wished to return to Lake Tai. One morning, as he was walking along the riverbank, he asked if there were any boats bound for Lake Xiu.
The boatman replied, "I am on a boat heading for Changzhou and Runzhou. Duanke said with delight, "That will do," and boarded at the stern.
When Gao You’s Qin Guan Shao-you heard of his lofty realization, he invited him to ascend the seat at Guanghui Temple. Duanke pointed to himself with his hand and said, "Heaven."
Above, there is no moon that is its equal; among men, there is but a single monk. In this hall, the wind is cold and still; through the ages, the meaning remains clear. Shao You nodded in agreement.
Zhiyuan was highly self-regarding and claimed his own excellence, speaking with strange and extraordinary words—a man of transcendent spirit.

His teeth had been ailing for a long time without healing, so he told the assembly, "Tomorrow I shall pass away. The assembly took it to be mere idle talk, yet they requested him to speak a verse. Zhiyuan asked for a brush.
A large inscription reads: "Master Duan is far too indolent; before he dies, his teeth will already have rotted away.

When he goes to the hall with the assembly during the two periods of the day, he can never manage to catch up with the gruel and rice. It would be better for him to die now; then he could sleep forever, unconcerned with anything at all.
First, he need not attend to the officials; second, he need not eat gruel and rice. At the fifth watch, he passed away. [End of] reading.
In the seventy-second year of the era, he was enshrined in Eastern Wu as a "Wandering Sage" (Sǎnshèng).
The eulogy states: "I was exiled overseas for three years before returning. The monastic groves had suddenly declined, and many elders had passed away.
Everywhere I went, there were only young practitioners filling the roads; they all ate their fill and engaged in groundless idle talk. He sighed deeply.
The two masters, Zhenghuang Niuzhu and Duanshizi, were both young in the monastic community thirty years ago;
yet their lofty character and refined style were already such as this—how much more so for those who have transmitted the Dharma and saved sentient beings!
Therefore, I have recorded the general outlines of these two gentlemen’s lives, so that the talented of future generations may examine them.
Biographical Record of the Venerable Master Duan’s Deeds and Conduct,
written and calligraphed by Liu Tao, a local of the commandery,
serving as the Acting Director General of the Judicial Introspection Office for the Eastern Route of Huainan (with the temporary rank of Chaoqing Lang and the borrowed rank of Zi-jin Yu-dai).
The late Chan Master Wushan Duan of the Song dynasty was named Jingduan, with the courtesy name Mingbiao. His secular surname was Qiu, and he was a native of Guian in Wuxing.
The Chancellor, Prince Shu, whose mastery of moral cultivation resulted in his every utterance becoming a scripture, encompassed the nine schools of thought and especially relished the joy of Chan.
Upon frequently seeing the Master’s verses and eulogies, he praised them, saying: "Only one who possesses a fundamental basis can be like this."—Recorded by Guanwen Lü.

The Grand Marshal (Taishou) took great interest in the inner scriptures (Buddhism) and produced many treatises and writings; yet among the monastics of the realm, few were able to receive his seal of approval.

Once, while traveling through Mount Wu, he halted his boat to visit [the Master]. Their words accorded perfectly. When the Master was exiled to Xuancheng, the Grand Marshal repeatedly sent letters to invite him, hosting him for several months.
Prime Minister Zhang Shen-gong, whose spiritual acumen was lofty and formidable—a true "Dragon Gate" of his generation—submitted a memorial requesting that the Master transmit the Dharma.
At the Lingshan Monastery, he was granted an imperial robe by decree; yet he remained there for many years, never yielding even slightly during his discussions on the Way with various dignitaries.
He drifted like floating clouds, coming and going as he pleased, never once begrudging his reputation or status, nor showing any change in his expression or speech for the sake of name or rank.
Given that the Three Dukes held him in such high esteem, his mastery of the Way can be believed without further words. And so it was.

That his lofty character and enduring legacy have been transmitted to future generations is beyond dispute. When he first resided at Shoujing Monastery in Changxing, there was one known as Houtou who had begun spreading his teachings in Jiahe;
his delusions were seducing the ignorant masses, and his fraudulent deceptions were flourishing. People from several prefectures offered him donations in mountain-like heaps.
Just as he was passing through the borders of this county, he saw the Master in the Buddha Hall. The Master struck Houtou on the head. Houtou—

[The opponent] was utterly unable to fathom [the Master’s meaning]. His face turned crimson and he remained speechless. The Master looked at him and said, "You have the head of a dragon but the tail of a snake.

Thereupon, the man, covered in shame and perspiration, fled to the seat of Master Lü. Once, when the Master encountered a sorcerer, everyone considered him a divine anomaly; yet the Master refuted him with a single word.
He immediately recognized the man’s falsehood and no longer spoke with him; later, the man was executed. Such instances of his lofty discernment and far-reaching insight were generally like this.
Later, when he arrived at the capital, Chan Master Yuanzhao was still at Hui-lin Monastery. The Master went there to pay his respects.
Yuanzhao greeted him, saying, "Are you not Master Duan? The Master assumed the posture of a lion. Yuanzhao then tested him with colloquial expressions, and the Master responded accordingly.
He followed this with a verse, and Yuanzhao smiled and consented. At that time, Minister Shen was presiding over the administration;

hearing of this, he wished to retain the Master at the capital, but the Master departed for his place of residence without informing him—just as in the cases of Shousheng, Xi Yu, Xiaogang, Zhang Fa, and others.
He would depart immediately upon not finding his purpose fulfilled, despite people vying to detain him. He did not stay.
He looked back with longing. From birth, he yearned for the Buddha; at six years of age, he left his home. He was diligent in his recitations.
His preceptor Baoxian frequently wished to ordain him, but it was not his wish. At twenty-six, he finally passed the examination by means of a treatise.

Having received full ordination, he first followed the master Jingjue Renyue to study the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school. While listening to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he reached the seventh [chapter].

He investigated the location of the mind and distinguished the seeing through the "eight returns. He composed a verse and prostrated himself before him. Jingjue read it and said, "Go now. You shall attain the Dharma through Chan.
Later, he went to visit Chan Master Baojue Qiyue. Within the master’s room, he attained silent realization;

immediately stepping out from under the platform, he turned his body and threw himself down. The assembly was struck with wonder and amazement. Afterwards, while watching a performance, he arrived at the scene where they were performing...
Shizi was exceptionally perceptive and quick-witted; thus, during the course of dialogues, he often assumed a spirited and vigorous demeanor. For this reason, he was known as Master Shendi Shizi.
Although he had never formally studied poetry, he composed verses on the spot that were naturally melodic and all worthy of admiration.

These works became so popular they were "minced and broiled" for the public palate, such that many could recite them from memory. Some compared him to Hanshan and Shide, noting his ability to foresee events before they occurred.

Regarding the matter of his coming to welcome [the Master], it was as if their words spoken while on the human path were joined like the two halves of a tally; nor could anyone find grounds to question it.
Upon returning, he resided at Wushan Temple. As provisions for food were insufficient, he would frequently board a small boat to travel wherever he intended to go.

When the boatman told him that the wind was contrary and they could not proceed, the Master said, "Where can one go so as to be with the wind? The boatman pointed toward the direction [he wished to take], whereupon—
He drifted away on the wind, following his inspiration. Before his feet had even reached the shore, those on the bank saw him from afar and vied with one another to welcome and prostrate before him.

He returned home laden with offerings of grain, yet within his paper robes there was not a single hair’s breadth of stored wealth. Whenever someone gave him something, he would immediately distribute it;

even when it came to the depths of winter and those seeking warmth from the cold came to him with tattered cotton and coarse wool, he wished to wrap himself in those very rags, and upon hearing of this, people would immediately send him new clothing.
He changed his ways. Some discussed how his request for a neighbor’s help was an act of kindness that seemed to border on seeking fame. The Master said, "Not so. I was naked and exposed;
if people felt pity for me, it was because otherwise he would have frozen to death. His intentions were often of this nature.
Although his conduct appeared like play, free and unrestrained without any constraints, he recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* without ever failing to do so.

Day by day he maintained his precepts with such purity that he never once violated them. He served his parents with the utmost filial piety, supporting them until the end of their lives; when they died, he buried them on the side of a mountain.

He took pity on the afflicted and was mindful of the poor, transmitting medical formulas and dispensing medicine without ever growing weary despite his advanced age. He styled himself the Monk Anxian (Peaceful Leisure).

Wearing straw sandals and carrying a *jiǎngzhàng* staff, whenever he encountered a scenic spot by a stream or mountain, he would don a raincoat and a bamboo hat, singing songs like a fisherman; thus, people were suddenly able to find peace.

Those afflicted by the heat of distress suddenly attained coolness; those in confinement and hardship briefly found ease and comfort. Wherever he went, his worldly ambitions were exhausted and he desired to return;

though eminent officials and high-ranking ministers offered him gold to detain him upon reaching Wuxing, he did not linger for even a moment. When the boat reached Wuxing, these great lords and dignitaries [followed].
He first inquired after his teacher’s well-being. He then prepared two earthenware vessels, saying, "When I die, bury me in these.

Having been free from illness or distress, on the fifth day of the twelfth month in the second year of the Chongning era, he suddenly said to the assembly of monks, "The time for my karmic conditions to end has arrived today.
He requested hot water for a bath, composed a verse to bid farewell to the assembly, sang several verses of the "Fisherman's Song," and with a smile, adjusted his robes.
He passed away while sitting in the lotus posture upon his robe. He was immediately interred in a ceramic vessel beneath Guiyun Hermitage;
this was indeed the seventh day of the first month of the following year. His secular age was seventy-four, and his monastic seniority was forty-nine years.

The Master had originally received his training at Jiekong Temple on Mount Wu; however, his disciples abandoned the fundamentals for the superficial, violating righteousness and destroying the precepts, committing every kind of transgression imaginable.

The Master had been away from the mountain for a long time pursuing his studies. Upon his return, everything was discarded; no pungent foods or vessels containing meat were permitted to enter the gate, and he remained strictly separated from the laity.
He first invited the lecturer Lingzhao to serve as his instructor for his studies. Subsequently, he obtained the support of the layman Fangyang, Mr.
Lu Yiyeweng, who acted both as an external patron and an internal collaborator. Together they sought provisions for the Sangha and mended all deficiencies, a tradition that continues to this day.
It subsequently became a renowned monastery for the pure assembly. He ordained forty-four disciples, including Ruosun, Changzhao, Zongli, and Zongjian;

all of them, through their learning, transmitted the Dharma and established monastic communities, becoming famous in their time. When I was still a youth with hair hanging down my forehead, the Master looked upon me once and immediately marveled at my extraordinary nature.
Later, when I had the misfortune of passing the imperial examinations, the court appointed me to an external post where I was left in idleness and underwent various hardships. Every time...

Whenever he traveled with his teacher, he would invariably say, "When I die, you must erect a stele for me. Long after his teacher had entered *nirvāṇa*, as time passed and circumstances shifted, he looked back and felt regret that this wish remained unfulfilled.
Zongjian (Zongmi) then drafted the beginning and end of the inscription; in a single night, the composition was complete, and he appended a preface to it. The epitaph reads:
"From Chan to the Exoteric Teachings, it is like setting forth myriad phenomena side by side; yet when they encounter a mirror, they are all reflected therein."
Thus, where could one go that is not essential? From teaching to Chan, it is like sailing with the wind while the waves are calm, yet pulling with an oar;
one encounters the source from either side, just as Master Duan, who was thoroughly learned in the sutras and śāstras, yet attained the fish-trap and rabbit-snares through his own realization.
Indeed, there is the divine awakening of Master Bao, the subtle words of Hanshan, the patched robe of Puhua, and the fishing pole of Chuanzi.
As for those things that can be compared through outward form, one may perceive the person; as for those things that cannot be grasped, who can know their heavenly nature?
Recorded by Zongjian, Dharma Master Zhengu, Abbot of the Juewu Teaching Monastery and lineage descendant of the Tiantai teachings;
carved by Niu Wan of Yangxian, together with his younger brother Ningmu, who set up this stone.
Epitaph for the Late Master Duan, the Anxian Worthy of the Song Dynasty.
Composed and calligraphed by Lin Zhan, Chamberlain of the Court of Audience, newly acting Military Commissioner of Jiangyin Prefecture, concurrently in charge of Agricultural Encouragement,
and recipient of the Scarlet Fish Bag.

Lin Shu, a recipient of the title of Chaoqing Lang, serving as a Counselor to the Pacification Commission for the Eastern Route of the Prefecture, and a wearer of the crimson fish-pendant, was a seventh-generation descendant of Master Zishen of Xiekong Monastery on Mount Wu.
Because his master Jiao resided at Shaofang Monastery, he followed [the master] Kan. By means of...
The messenger reported with deep emotion: "My ancestor passed away in the second year of the Chongning era and was buried behind the Golden Hall.

In the past, you, Master, presided over this mountain, opening a vast Dharma assembly and gathering a sea-like multitude from the ten directions. You were as inseparable from this mountain as its very name, which spread throughout the world.
Yet since your passing, the chanting of sutras and the offering of incense and lamps have become as thin as a single thread, both among the scholar-officials and our own followers."
Furthermore, people came to pay their respects, wandering back and forth above and below, lamenting that the Buddha-dharma was not flourishing.

Those skilled in the arts of *yinyang* and geomancy (*zhaixiang*) considered the master’s burial site to be inherently auspicious; they attributed the lack of prosperity to the fact that the orientation and alignment of the grave did not conform to ancient laws.
When the local magistrate heard of this, he requested a change of location. The Daoist Shi Hao offered his labor and resources to construct a pavilion there.

In front [of the tomb], he maintained the old plaque of his ancestral hermitage, naming it "Returning Clouds" (Guīyún), and made solemn offerings there. Previously, Wenhui had personally received the master’s transmission;

sixty years later, he opened the view of my tomb. When the appointed time arrived, the disciples looked at one another and said, "We dare to take advantage of this moment so as not to let fall our ancestral master’s command.
Thus, on the twenty-first day of the first lunar month in the year of Gengxu...
On that day, the work was commenced with the mobilization of craftsmen who dug into the earth. People from near and far flocked there, and the onlookers were as dense as a wall.

Yet the bricks did not shift, and the ceramic vessels remained exactly as they were. Upon opening them to look inside, not a single object was found. The fourfold assembly clamored with excitement, marveling at such a rare occurrence. They wept together in sorrow, saying, "This must be recorded;
for while the Tathāgata dwelt in the world, he expounded upon the four great elements and the six sense objects."
The union of the internal and external is like an illusion. The Master tied the "hare-head" cloth, untied the "hare-net," and shattered all attachment to a self.

Furthermore, he taught the six perfections and myriad practices for the sake of both oneself and others; like a reflection in a mirror, when the image vanishes, the mirror becomes empty, thereby shattering all attachment to phenomena.
Chan Master Duan Gong, in his youth, observed a lion’s performance and attained realization of samādhi. Speaking in both Hu and Han tongues, he would lift them upright and cast them upside down;
they were driven like the wind and swept away like lightning, beyond the reach of inquiry.

Strange and wondrous, manifesting ten thousand forms in a single kṣaṇa, those with minds were utterly deceived, and those with eyes were completely hoodwinked. Once the illusory body has perished, the illusory dharmas remain forever for billions of kalpas.
Ashes turn to extinction; what is called "birth" is termed the "dispersion of the sage," and what is called "death" is termed "corpse-liberation.
To deliberate in such a manner is to cause the illusory dharma to blaze ever more fiercely. Linji harbored doubts regarding Puhua, and Dahui truly praised the golden-haired lion.

As for Hengtang, he did not harbor such doubts; yet he could not avoid offering praise after praise, uttering a verse that said: "The lion in the mirror is distinct; this blinking of eyes and raising of eyebrows is death."
Rest! For a thousand ages no one has known this meaning: a single cry of a fisherman’s song under the bright moon in autumn.
The Tripitaka Master praises the true likeness of Master Duan of Zheyou:

A lion of the Southland, his roar startles the gates of heaven; In the empty mountains he occasionally displays his prowess; When emerging from meditative concentration, he again lets out a low growl.
Startling the slumbering multitudes of sentient beings, they awaken clearly to their original truth. Why must one be a "Foal of the Horse" (Mākaṇḍika) to trample the people of the world underfoot?
Chan Master Dahuì of Jing Mountain praised the Master’s portrait:
"The lion’s skin has been worn well; at the hour of the tiger, going and staying are swept away by the wind. He called out to Official Zhang, treating him with contempt.
Old Yuanzhao did not rely on the Master; with two fists, he struck him down. Turning his head, he cursed the "demon-monk" with a single phrase.
Look only at these few moves; there is no need to inquire about his Zen or the Way. This one is a true cub of the golden-maned lion;
the foxes and jackals are merely barking and howling in vain.
Master Dànfēnbiànzhēn’s Eulogy for the Master’s Portrait:
A vagabond on the streets, devoid of sincerity; He knew only to indulge his whims and give rein to ignorance. The lineages of the Five Houses are difficult to gather;
Who recognizes that he has continued the ancestral lamp?
The Recorded Sayings of Master Anxian. Prior to the Jiading era, Master Jiao had provided the funds to carve the printing blocks; however, he passed away before the project was completed.

Out of reverence for his late master’s sincere aspiration, Emperor Shizu returned the robes and alms-bowl [he had received] and commissioned artisans to engrave the woodblocks, so that they might be widely circulated.
Dated the fifteenth day of the sixth month in the third year of the Duanping era, the Bingshen year.
